props.title: It Might Get Loud
props.initialSlug: Jimmy Page, The Edge, and Jack White discuss guitar

sections.content: It Might Get Loud revolutionized music documentaries by uniting three guitar legends from different eras - Jimmy Page (Led Zeppelin), The Edge (U2), and Jack White (The White Stripes). Unlike traditional rock docs like Don't Look Back (1967) or The Last Waltz (1978), director Davis Guggenheim strips away the excess to focus purely on artistic creation and the electric guitar's evolution. The film's genius lies in its intimate "guitar summit" format, letting these masters share techniques, stories, and philosophies while jamming together.

sections.content: The film's approach to musical innovation mirrors other groundbreaking docs like Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002) and Muscle Shoals (2013). Each guitarist represents a different relationship with technology - Page's analog mastery, Edge's effects-driven soundscapes, and White's raw minimalism. Their contrasting approaches echo larger shifts in music production explored in docs like Sound City (2013), where Dave Grohl examines analog recording's decline.

What sets It Might Get Loud apart is its focus on process over personality. While films like The Devil and Daniel Johnston (2005) or Amy (2015) dig into musicians' personal struggles, Guggenheim keeps the spotlight on creative methodology. The film's most powerful moments come when these icons drop their legends and simply geek out over guitar riffs, proving that at heart, they're still students of their craft. sections.content: The film's innovative structure influenced later music docs like Foo Fighters: Back and Forth (2011) and The Sound of My Voice (2019), showing how technical craft discussions can be as compelling as behind-the-scenes drama. When Page demonstrates the opening riff to "Whole Lotta Love" or White builds a guitar from scratch, we're watching master classes in musical innovation that transcend typical rock documentary tropes.
